slowest_experiments.label: Exp 308: JEPA fast-path gate integration — checkpoint (tests failing)
slowest_experiments.likely_cause: Third consecutive milestone appearance for this experiment. Originally run pre-.37, re-touched during the .38 retroactive DualGPU sweep, and re-touched again in .39 during the BatchedInferenceRunner migration sprint (Exp 518) or RETRO-052 harness sweep. Each re-entry pays full context-reconstruction overhead: reading the 3900+ test suite state, triaging pre-existing failures from newly broken tests, and recommitting. The tests-failing checkpoint state was not cleared in .38 and the experiment was never marked 'legacy_modernized'. This experiment must receive a definitive one-time modernization pass that marks it complete and prevents future re-entry: BatchedInferenceRunner migration, DualGPU device assignment, VRAM pre-check guard, and a 'legacy_modernized=true' result field.

slowest_experiments.label: Exp 425: Conductor timeout watchdog — RETRO-003 (17+ milestone carry)
slowest_experiments.likely_cause: Third consecutive milestone appearance in the slowest-5. Exp 425 implemented ExperimentTimeoutWatchdog in .37 (RETRO-003 closure) but continues to generate re-entry overhead in subsequent milestones. The likely trigger is the retroactive sweeps (DualGPU harness in .38, batching migration in .39) re-visiting this experiment to apply infrastructure upgrades. Because Exp 425 is an infrastructure experiment itself (it implements watchdog timeouts), every sweep that touches infrastructure scripts will visit it. The pattern: experiments that implement infrastructure components are visited by every subsequent infrastructure sweep, compounding re-entry costs. Resolution: mark Exp 425 as 'infrastructure_component=watchdog, not a subject for future sweeps' in a manifest file so the conductor does not re-visit it.

slowest_experiments.label: Exp 260 partial: CPU-bound benchmark proves GPU need
slowest_experiments.likely_cause: Third consecutive milestone appearance. The VRAM pre-check inserted at model.load() (RETRO-051, Exp 513, Phase 1 of .39) was the stated fix for this class of wasted execution. If Exp 513 ran successfully and JITVRAMCheck is now deployed, then Exp 260's 74-minute re-appearance means either: (a) the VRAM check was not applied retroactively to this legacy script, or (b) the retroactive sweep re-ran Exp 260 before the check was in place. The residual lesson is that legacy scripts require explicit opt-in to new gates — deploying JITVRAMCheck at the framework level does not automatically inject it into pre-Exp-513 scripts unless the modernization manifest is applied. Exp 260 must receive the full legacy_modernized treatment and be excluded from future sweeps.

slowest_experiments.label: Exp 226: Full 164-problem HumanEval with PBT
slowest_experiments.likely_cause: Third consecutive milestone appearance in the slowest-5. Exp 518 (BatchedInferenceRunner migration sprint, Phase 4 of .39) was explicitly designed to patch the top-20 legacy scripts including this one. If Exp 226 still appears at 73 min despite the migration sprint, one of three things happened: (a) Exp 518 was deferred or incomplete, (b) the migration was applied but did not produce measurable speedup on HumanEval (unlikely — PBT scoring on 164 sequential problems is highly parallelizable), or (c) the slowest-5 data captures the pre-migration run that was re-verified during the sprint setup. The fact that three of the five slowest .39 experiments (Exps 226, 260, 308) also appeared in the slowest-5 of .37 and .38 is the strongest possible signal that the Exp 518 migration sprint either did not run or did not reach these three targets.

slowest_experiments.label: Exp 309: Tier 3 end-to-end self-learning — checkpoint (tests failing)
slowest_experiments.likely_cause: New addition to the slowest-5 (replaces Exp 221 from .38, which was migrated or fell below the 66-min threshold). Exp 309 is a Tier 3 end-to-end self-learning experiment — one of the highest-complexity experiment types in the pipeline, combining constraint addition from memory, JitRL updates, and NUP probe feedback. A checkpoint-with-tests-failing state indicates an interrupted conductor run that left the system in an inconsistent state, similar to Exp 308. The 66-minute cost is primarily context reconstruction: determining which of the many interacting components in the Tier 3 stack caused the test failure requires re-reading the full dependency chain (constraint_addition.py, jitrl.py, nup_probe.py, fover_annotator.py). The ExperimentTimeoutWatchdog (Exp 425) should prevent new Tier 3 experiments from running past the 45-min cap, but it cannot retroactively clean up experiments that predate its deployment.

bottlenecks_identified: Zombie process regression at milestone close: PID 342137 holds 12434MB on GPU 0 and 15602MB on GPU 1 (28036MB total, ~28GB across both cards) at 0% compute utilization. Wall time for the process is 847 seconds (~14 minutes), meaning it was launched near the end of the milestone and never cleaned up. This is a structural regression from .38's clean 2MB close state. The .38 retro celebrated RETRO-048 resolution (conductor VRAM freed); .39 close shows a new zombie pattern — not the conductor, but an experiment script that loaded both models (Qwen ~12GB on GPU 0, Gemma ~15GB on GPU 1) and exited without calling torch.cuda.empty_cache() or del model. The GPU monitor correctly flags it: 'Process may be idle — consider freeing memory.' The fix is mandatory model cleanup at experiment exit — either a context manager in ExperimentTemplate.teardown() or a registered atexit hook. Without this, .40 will open with 28GB of VRAM blocked from the first experiment.

Legacy pre-400 experiments dominate the slowest-5 for the THIRD consecutive milestone: Exps 226, 260, 308 appear in all three of the .37, .38, and .39 slowest-5 lists. Each milestone they cost 70-105 minutes of re-entry overhead. Over three milestones, these three experiments alone have consumed approximately 3 × (73+74+105) = 756 minutes — more than 12 hours — of milestone wall time from re-entry overhead alone. The Exp 518 BatchedInferenceRunner migration sprint was designed to break this cycle, but the recurrence suggests it either did not complete, was scoped too narrowly, or was applied without the 'legacy_modernized=true' flag that would prevent conductor re-selection. This is the single highest-leverage bottleneck in the system: closing these three experiments permanently would remove ~750 min of legacy overhead from the next three-milestone window.

BatchedInferenceRunner migration sprint (Exp 518) completion status unknown: Exp 518 was Phase 4 of .39 and was the primary mechanism to migrate the top-20 legacy scripts. If Exp 518 ran but was scoped only to new scripts (not retroactively to Exps 226/260/308), the sprint created infrastructure without closing the legacy backlog. If Exp 518 was deferred, the 77-violation backlog documented in Exp 481 persists untouched for the third consecutive milestone. The recurrence of Exps 226/260/308 in the slowest-5 is circumstantial evidence that the sprint either was incomplete or scoped too narrowly. Before .40 planning, the result file for Exp 518 must be read to determine which of the 77 violating scripts were actually migrated.

DualGPU parallelism: models loaded but compute serialized. GPU 1 shows 15612MB of VRAM used at close (64%) — significantly higher than .38's clean 2MB close. This confirms that .39 experiments were actually loading models onto GPU 1, which is a structural improvement over .37 (DualGPURunner not wired) and .38 (DualGPU sweep completed but compute not verified). However, GPU 1 is at 0% utilization at close, indicating the loaded model is idle. One of two patterns: (a) experiments load Model A on GPU 0 and Model B on GPU 1 serially, then run all inference on GPU 0 before switching to GPU 1 — no actual parallel execution; or (b) the last experiment loaded both models and exited without completing inference (zombie scenario). Either way, the 15612MB on GPU 1 at 0% compute represents unused parallel capacity. The DualGPU controlled test (Exp 517, Phase 3) was designed to verify actual parallel execution; its result file must confirm whether parallel forward passes were achieved.

RETRO carry-limit enforcement still absent: Exps 308 and 425 appear in the slowest-5 for the third consecutive milestone, and Exp 309 joins them as a new checkpoint-failure entry. The two-milestone RETRO carry limit was suggested in .37, recommended again in .38, and not implemented in either milestone. The .39 slowest-5 now contains THREE checkpoint-failure experiments (308, 309, and implicitly 260 which ran to a gpu_required partial result). The carry-limit would not directly fix these experiments, but it would prevent new RETRO items from accumulating the same pattern — each open RETRO that runs past its carry limit eventually appears in a slowest-5 as a context-reconstruction cost. The enforcement mechanism needed is a conductor-level check that escalates any RETRO item entering its second milestone without a scheduled resolution experiment.

JIT VRAM check (RETRO-051) coverage gap: the zombie process at close (28GB, 0% compute) demonstrates that the JITVRAMCheck deployed in Phase 1 (Exp 513) does not cover the teardown path — only the setup path (checking VRAM before model.load()). An experiment can pass the JIT pre-check, load models successfully, and then exit without freeing VRAM, leaving the memory locked for the next experiment. The RETRO-051 fix was necessary but not sufficient. The full fix is: JIT pre-check at load() AND guaranteed cleanup at exit. The ExperimentTemplate must include a teardown() method that is called regardless of experiment success or failure (try/finally pattern).

Context-load overhead persists across milestone boundaries: the planning session for .39 (2026-04-19T14:00:00Z) and the .38 retro session ran as separate context loads earlier in the same day. The .39 retro (this document) runs as a third separate context load. Three distinct context-load events paying 10-15 minutes of file-read overhead each adds 30-45 minutes of non-experiment wall time per milestone. The consolidation suggestion from .37 and .38 retros has not been adopted. The pattern is now documented in three consecutive retros without resolution — it qualifies as a persistent process debt item that should be added to the RETRO registry (RETRO-053).
improvements_suggested: Add mandatory model cleanup to ExperimentTemplate.teardown() with try/finally guarantee: implement del model; torch.cuda.empty_cache(); gc.collect() in a finally block that runs regardless of experiment success, failure, or timeout. The zombie at .39 close (PID 342137, 28GB, 0% util) is the direct evidence that this path is missing. The ExperimentTimeoutWatchdog (Exp 425) correctly kills the experiment process on timeout, but does not guarantee GPU VRAM release if the process exit path skips cleanup. The teardown() call must be registered with atexit in ExperimentTemplate.__init__ so that even os._exit() calls cannot bypass it. Expected impact: eliminates all zombie VRAM carryover between experiments. Cost: 1-2 hour implementation in experiment_template.py + 30 tests.

Create a 'legacy_modernized' manifest and apply it to Exps 226, 260, 308, 309 in a single dedicated sweep: these four experiments have collectively appeared in the slowest-5 across three milestones, consuming an estimated 900+ minutes of re-entry overhead. A single targeted sweep that applies ALL of the following to each experiment — BatchedInferenceRunner migration, DualGPU device assignment (cuda:0/cuda:1 explicit), VRAM pre-check guard (JITVRAMCheck), checkpoint-failure state cleared, and 'legacy_modernized=true' in result file — and then writes them to a conductor-level exclusion manifest ('do not re-select these experiments for future sweeps') would close this drain permanently. Budget: 4-6 hours for four experiments. ROI: eliminates ~300 min/milestone of recurring overhead for the next 3+ milestones.

Verify Exp 518 BatchedInferenceRunner migration sprint result and complete the remaining violations: before .40 planning, read results/experiment_518*.json to determine which of the 77 violating scripts were migrated. If fewer than 20 were completed, re-scope the sprint as the FIRST experiment of .40 (not a new-research experiment) and require it to reach the top-20 slowest scripts by wall-time × frequency product. The sprint must not be considered complete until all three of the recurring slowest-5 targets (Exps 226/260/308) have 'batching_migrated=true' in their result files.

Verify Exp 517 DualGPU controlled test result for actual parallel execution evidence: the GPU state at .39 close (GPU 1 at 15612MB, 0% compute) is ambiguous — it could mean parallel loading achieved but serial inference, or model loaded without inference started. Read results/experiment_517*.json for: (a) wall-clock time of parallel vs serial run, (b) GPU 1 utilization percentage during inference (must be >0%), (c) throughput improvement factor. If Exp 517 confirmed parallel loading but not parallel inference, open RETRO-054 specifically for parallel forward-pass execution — distinct from RETRO-052 (DualGPU device assignment). These are separate problems requiring separate fixes.

Register context-load consolidation as RETRO-053 and schedule it in .40: three consecutive retros (this included) have documented the multi-session context-load overhead without resolution. The lack of a RETRO number has prevented it from entering the formal tracking system and competing for milestone priority. Open RETRO-053: 'End-of-milestone documentation passes run as three separate sessions (retro + planning + retro write), paying triple context-load overhead. Fix: merge into a single combined session with explicit agenda: (1) write retro JSON, (2) update ops docs, (3) plan next milestone.' Expected savings: 30-45 min per milestone from eliminated redundant file reads.

Enforce two-milestone RETRO carry limit by adding it as a pre-flight check in the conductor: before generating a .40 roadmap, the conductor must enumerate all open RETRO items, identify which are entering their third or higher milestone of carry, and schedule at least one as a critical-path Phase 1 item — before any new research. Currently the .39 milestone close has at least RETRO-031, RETRO-033, RETRO-038, RETRO-039, RETRO-049, RETRO-051 (partially addressed), RETRO-052 (partially addressed) all in multi-milestone carry. In .40, the oldest unresolved RETRO must close. Recommended: formalize the carry-limit as a JSON field in each RETRO item ('opened_milestone', 'carry_count') and fail the roadmap validation step if any item has carry_count >= 2 without a scheduled resolution experiment.

Add 'experiment close state' verification to the milestone close checklist: the GPU monitor data at close shows PID 342137 with 847 seconds of wall time — approximately 14 minutes, meaning it was launched near the end of the milestone. A milestone close checklist (suggested in .38, still not formalized) should include: (1) run gpu_monitor.py and assert all GPU utilization == 0% AND all VRAM <= 500MB; (2) if any process is found, kill it and log the PID and VRAM footprint to ops/known-issues.md; (3) do not write the retro JSON until the GPU state is clean. This converts zombie detection from a lagging indicator (discovered in the retro) to a leading indicator (discovered and remediated before the retro).

Prioritize RETRO-033 (live 100q verify-repair positive result) as the first .40 experiment: the .38 retro made this same recommendation. The .38 close state was clean (2MB VRAM); the .39 close state is not clean (28GB zombie). Before launching the credibility benchmark in .40, the teardown() fix must be deployed first — run the benchmark immediately after confirming GPU state is clean. If RETRO-033 continues to miss in .40, escalate immediately to root-cause analysis (is the verify-repair pipeline itself producing measurable improvements at 100q scale, or is the mechanism incomplete?) rather than deferring for an eighth consecutive milestone.
estimated_time_savings_rationale: Compared to the .39 baseline of 4577 min / 375 experiments: (1) Mandatory model teardown/cleanup hook eliminating zombie VRAM carry: the zombie at .39 close (PID 342137, 28GB, 14 min) would have blocked the first .40 experiment from loading any model without the zombie kill. Each such mid-milestone blockage historically costs 30-74 min (the Exp 260 deferred_to_gpu pattern). Preventing 1-2 such blockages per milestone saves ~60-120 min — approximately 2-3% of total wall time. (2) Legacy modernization of Exps 226/260/308/309 via single dedicated sweep: at ~75 min each per milestone appearance, four experiments appearing once per milestone (conservative) = 300 min. A one-time 4-6 hour modernization investment (240-360 min) that removes them permanently saves ~300 min × subsequent milestones. For .40 alone: ~6.5% savings vs .39 baseline. (3) True DualGPU parallel inference for dual-model benchmarks: GPU 1 now has models loaded (15612MB at close confirms device assignment working), but 0% compute means serial execution. Parallelizing inference on dual-model benchmarks (40% of experiments by count) could yield near-2x speedup on those experiments — conservatively, a 1.5x speedup on 40% yields ~13% improvement on those experiments, or ~5% on total wall time. (4) RETRO carry-limit enforcement: prevents future context-debt-multiplier events (RETRO-003 cost ~50 min extra due to 17-milestone carry). One such event avoided per milestone = ~1%. (5) RETRO-053 context-load consolidation: three sessions → one saves ~30 min per milestone = ~0.7%. Combined: approximately 15-20% additional savings. Historical calibration: .37 estimated 25% for .38, achieved 4% (RETRO-048 resolution dominated). .38 estimated 18% for .39, achieved 1.4% (4639→4577 min, -62 min). The pattern is that estimated savings consistently exceed realized savings by ~10-15 percentage points because architectural changes (DualGPU parallel, teardown hooks) are harder to implement and adopt than procedural ones. Conservative estimate for .40: 15-20%, with 5-8% realistically achievable if teardown hook and legacy modernization sweep are completed.

gpu_state_at_milestone_close.gpu0_assessment: Regression from .38 close (2MB, 0% util). PID 342137 holds 12434MB on GPU 0 at 0% utilization — a model is loaded (likely Qwen ~12GB based on VRAM footprint) but not actively inferring. The process has been running for ~14 minutes with 1159.8 CPU seconds consumed (1.37 CPU-hours / 0.235 hours = 5.8x CPU-to-wall ratio, indicating multi-core batch work or JAX compilation that completed and left the model resident). Temperature at 49C is safe (well below 80C thermal gate). But the 12444MB footprint means only 12132MB free — insufficient to load a second large model. The next experiment in .40 will hit OOM if it attempts to load any model larger than ~12GB without first killing PID 342137. This is the same failure mode as .37's RETRO-048, re-emerging from a different root cause (experiment teardown failure vs conductor VRAM).
gpu_state_at_milestone_close.gpu1_assessment: Significant regression from .38 close (2MB, 0% util). PID 342137 holds 15602MB on GPU 1 at 0% utilization — this is consistent with Gemma4-27B quantized (~15GB in INT4/GGUF format) loaded but idle. The 15612MB footprint leaves only 8964MB free on GPU 1. The fact that GPU 1 holds MORE VRAM than GPU 0 is notable: this confirms that the DualGPU harness work (RETRO-052, Exp 517) achieved model loading on cuda:1 — a structural advance over .38. However, both models being idle at 0% compute means the parallel execution was either completed (and cleanup was skipped) or the experiment was interrupted during setup. Either way, GPU 1 is now the larger VRAM holder at close.
gpu_state_at_milestone_close.improvement_vs_38: GPU state at .39 close is substantially worse than .38 close. .38 close: GPU 0 at 0% util, 2MB; GPU 1 at 0% util, 2MB. .39 close: GPU 0 at 0% util, 12444MB; GPU 1 at 0% util, 15612MB. Total VRAM used: 28056MB vs 4MB in .38 — a 7000x regression. The regression is not the conductor (RETRO-048 appears to remain resolved — no conductor VRAM signature) but an experiment process (PID 342137 from .venv) that loaded both models and did not clean up. The DualGPU activation (both models loaded simultaneously) is structurally an advance; the zombie cleanup failure is operationally a regression. The two are causally linked: activating DualGPU without a corresponding teardown hook creates the zombie pattern for every dual-model experiment that terminates abnormally.
gpu_state_at_milestone_close.thermal_gate_status: GPU 0 at 49C, GPU 1 at 47C — both well within the 80C gate threshold. No thermal risk. Temperatures are lower than .38 close (51-52C) despite higher VRAM load, suggesting both GPUs are in a post-inference cooling state after PID 342137 completed its compute work (~14 min ago).

retro_improvement_adoption.verdict: The critical architectural advances of .39 — JIT VRAM pre-check and DualGPU model loading — are real structural improvements over .38 and .37. GPU 1 holding 15602MB at close is evidence that actual dual-GPU operation was achieved for the first time in the project history. However, the missing teardown hook means DualGPU activation created a new zombie variant: instead of the conductor holding VRAM, experiment scripts now hold it. The adoption rate (60%, down from .38's 78%) reflects three concrete non-adoptions (batching migration, carry-limit, teardown hook) that each have direct performance consequences. The teardown hook is the highest-priority adoption for .40 — without it, the DualGPU advance becomes a liability at milestone close.

meta_reflection.dualgpu_activation_verdict: Partial success: model loading achieved, parallel execution not confirmed. The .39 close (GPU 1 at 15602MB, 0% util) proves that the DualGPU harness successfully loaded a second model on cuda:1 for the first time in project history. This is a meaningful structural advance over .37 (device_map='auto' with no explicit cuda:1) and .38 (sweep applied but no load confirmed). The outstanding gap: 0% GPU 1 utilization means inference ran on GPU 0 only, or ran to completion and the process is now zombie. The next step is explicit profiler evidence (nvidia-smi dmon or torch.profiler trace) showing both GPUs at >0% utilization simultaneously. Until that evidence exists, DualGPU is loading-confirmed but execution-unconfirmed.
meta_reflection.adoption_trend: Adoption rates: 0% (.33) → 50% (.35) → 60% (.36) → 100% (.37) → 78% (.38) → 60% (.39). The .39 dip from 78% to 60% reflects two structural non-adoptions: teardown hook and RETRO carry-limit. Both were recommended in .37, .38, and .39. Three consecutive non-adoptions of the same items is a process failure, not a prioritization trade-off. These items must be elevated to hard prerequisites for .40 rather than suggestions.
meta_reflection.wall_time_trend: Seven-milestone trajectory: .33=5002 → .34=4886 → .35=4948 → .36=4921 → .37=4833 → .38=4639 → .39=4577 min. Continued improvement but at a decelerating rate: .38 improved by -194 min (-4.0%), .39 improved by -62 min (-1.3%). Per-experiment average: .33=16.1 → .34=16.5 → .35=15.6 → .36=14.6 → .37=13.9 → .38=12.9 → .39=12.0 min. Consistent improvement; first time below 12 min. The deceleration in wall-time improvement despite increasing experiments (375 vs 359) indicates that per-experiment gains are being offset by experiment volume growth and legacy overhead. The next step-change improvement requires either DualGPU parallel execution (structural throughput gain) or elimination of the four recurring legacy experiments from future re-entry cycles.
meta_reflection.credibility_verdict: UNKNOWN at .39 close: Phase 2 (Exps 514-516) targeted RETRO-033/038/039 with clean VRAM (both GPUs should have been free after Exp 513 JIT check deployed). The zombie at close (PID 342137) was launched after the credibility benchmarks, so it should not have blocked them. Result files for Exps 514-516 must be checked. If deferred again: escalate to architectural root cause analysis — the verify-repair signal may be too small to measure at 100q scale, requiring a larger benchmark or a different metric.
meta_reflection.process_debt_vector: Three debt clusters persist: (1) Legacy experiment debt — Exps 226/260/308/309 dominating slowest-5 for 3rd consecutive milestone, requiring ~300 min/milestone in re-entry overhead; (2) Teardown debt — experiment processes not cleaning GPU memory, creating zombie patterns at close; (3) Documentation session debt — multi-session context-load overhead adding ~30-45 min/milestone. All three are addressable with concrete, bounded implementations. The fact that all three have been documented in three consecutive retros without resolution confirms that they require RETRO numbers, not just retro recommendations.

vs_prior_milestone.observation: Wall time decreased 1.3% (4639→4577 min) with 16 additional experiments (375 vs 359). Per-experiment average dropped from 12.9 to 12.0 min — a meaningful threshold crossed. However, the -62 min improvement is less than one-third of .38's -194 min improvement. The deceleration is consistent with the pattern: each milestone's big architectural unlock (RETRO-048 in .38, DualGPU loading in .39) produces an incremental but diminishing return. The next step-change — either parallel DualGPU inference or legacy experiment elimination — has not been unlocked yet. GPU state at close is significantly worse than .38 (28GB zombie vs 2MB clean), representing a structural regression that must be corrected before .40 begins.
